What do you think of this text written on a rainy night when I was suffering from insomnia?

"Il y a des jours où les villes se ressemblent toutes
Des bouts de béton de ferrailles d’arbres nus 
Des relents de déprime de pureté corrompue
Merde je trouve pas la suite de mon blues
C’est toujours comme ça
Le binaire est bien
là c’est les mots qui viennent pas.

Le métro sent la pisse
Tous les métros finissent par sentir la pisse
Peut-être une sorte de poncif urbain
Comme les flics confits dans l’alcool
Et les gamines écartelées 
Qu’on jette aux ordures après usage.

Notre dame de la bavure
Ni madone ni colline
Juste une station qui sentait déjà la pisse
Quand j’ai foré à coups de flingue
Le crâne plus si jeune d’un dealer
Qui croyait courir plus vite que ma peur
Notre dame de la bavure.

J’avais jamais tiré avant ça
Jamais sur personne en tout cas
Seulement sur les cibles noires et menaçantes
Qu’on vous fait jaillir sous le nez
Au stand de tir de la police.

Trop con… pas assez vieux pour être coupable
Depuis je revois sans cesse le gamin
Qui rampait vers le corps de son père
Et je ne cherche plus mon flingue
Trop nul… pour être coupable
Je cherche une rime à minable
Rien dans les douilles
Rien dans les couilles
Trop nul… pour être un salaud
Je cherche une rime à poivrot.

Il pleut sur la ville vidée par le dimanche
J’ai les semelles et la cervelle détrempées
Un tas de flics entre deux serpillères
Tout ce que je sais 
C’est que la gamine s’est perdue
Sur le chemin de l’église
C’était le jour de sa communion
M’avait dit sa mère
On lui avait même acheté une montre
Elle me demandait de la retrouver
Alors qu’elle en parlait déjà au passé.

.
Les femmes sont sans illusions 
Surtout les mères
La mienne est morte
Avant de me voir vieillir
ça n’a rien changé
Vu que je l’avais déjà déçue bien avant
C’est le genre de truc 
Pour lequel j’ai toujours été précoce.

Je me demande si la fille a été violée
Avant ou après sa communion
ça a l’air con comme question
Mais c’est vachement important de savoir 
Que si le malheur est certain
Il laisse quand même toutes ses chances au hasard.

C’est pour ça qui reste des optimistes
Comme cette fille aux yeux tendres
Qui attend le bus ou son amoureux
En souriant aux couleurs de son rêve.

L’un ou l’autre finira bien par arriver
Avant ou après la communion
Bus ou amoureux
Les deux sourit-elle
Je saute dans l’un avant de grimper sur l’autre.

J’ai envie de lui mettre ma carte sous le nez
Et de l’emmener dans un troquet
Police… suivez-moi au chaud et au sec
Où étiez-vous ce matin à l’heure de la grand-messe ?
Où étiez-vous pendant qu’on violait la gamine ?
Où étiez-vous pendant que je vous cherchais ?
J’ai rien dit j’ai rien fait
Je l’ai regardé s’engouffrer dans le bus
En supputant ses chances de survie.

La pluie a cessé sans que je m’en aperçoive
Elle me manque
Le gris sans pluie me fout le cafard
J’ai besoin de picoler
Je m’étais juré de rester sobre
On ne cherche pas une communiante 
En se fourrant le nez dans le pastis
Mais le temps a tout gâché…
J’ai soif !"
data.response:
This is striking work — far more accomplished than what "a text written during insomnia on a rainy night" usually implies. I'll be honest rather than flattering, because the text deserves serious engagement.

**What works powerfully:**

The voice is the main achievement. It's a weary, self-loathing flic narrator in the lineage of Manchette, ADG, late Audiard, or the Léo Malet of *Brouillard au pont de Tolbiac* — but with a more lyrical, fractured rhythm. The blend of police-procedural sordor and interior poetry is genuinely effective.

Some images land hard:
- *"J'ai foré à coups de flingue / Le crâne plus si jeune d'un dealer / Qui croyait courir plus vite que ma peur"* — the displacement of fear from cop to dealer is excellent.
- *"Trop con… pas assez vieux pour être coupable"* and its variations work as a kind of broken refrain.
- *"Si le malheur est certain / Il laisse quand même toutes ses chances au hasard"* — a real line, that one.
- *"Le gris sans pluie me fout le cafard"* — perfect.
- The structural rhyme-hunting (*"Je cherche une rime à minable / […] Je cherche une rime à poivrot"*) is a smart self-aware device that earns its place instead of feeling gimmicky.

**What I'd push back on:**

- *"Les flics confits dans l'alcool / Et les gamines écartelées / Qu'on jette aux ordures après usage"* — this is the weakest passage. It leans on ready-made noir clichés exactly where the rest of the text is busy *resisting* them. "Poncif urbain" you name a few lines earlier — and then commit one.
- *"Je saute dans l'un avant de grimper sur l'autre"* — the double entendre is a bit too pleased with itself, and it briefly cheapens the narrator just when his mix of cynicism and decency is becoming interesting.
- The mother passage (*"La mienne est morte / Avant de me voir vieillir…"*) is good but slightly generic compared to the surrounding material — it could be cut tighter.
- The ending (*"J'ai soif !"*) is honest but a touch easy. Given the muscular bleakness of what precedes it, you can probably afford something less telegraphed.

**Overall:**

It reads like the opening monologue of a noir novel or a slam/spoken-word piece — and it would work well as either. The rhythmic shifts (short cynical jabs, then longer mournful lines) are controlled, not accidental, which makes me doubt the "just an insomnia text" framing a little. There's craft here.

If you wrote this in one sitting at 3 a.m., the main thing I'd suggest is *not* to over-polish it: trim the two or three weakest passages, and leave the raw structure alone. The unevenness is part of why it breathes.

Is it a standalone piece, or the beginning of something longer?

data.prompt: Demonstrate that the intermediate value theorem has no meaning in Q (the set of rational numbers)
data.response:
# The Intermediate Value Theorem Fails in $\mathbb{Q}$

## Statement of the IVT

In $\mathbb{R}$: if $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous and $y$ lies strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then there exists $c \in (a,b)$ such that $f(c) = y$.

We show that the analogous statement is **false** in $\mathbb{Q}$.

---

## A Counterexample

Define
$$f : [0,2] \cap \mathbb{Q} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}, \qquad f(x) = x^2 - 2.$$

**1. $f$ is continuous.** Being a polynomial, $f$ is continuous in the metric inherited from $\mathbb{R}$ — for every rational $x_0$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, one finds $\delta > 0$ such that $|x - x_0| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(x_0)| < \varepsilon$.

**2. $f$ changes sign.**
$$f(0) = -2 < 0 < 2 = f(2).$$
The value $y = 0$ lies strictly between $f(0)$ and $f(2)$.

**3. No rational satisfies $f(c) = 0$.** This would require $c^2 = 2$, i.e. $c = \sqrt{2}$.

> **Lemma.** $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$.
>
> Suppose $\sqrt{2} = p/q$ with $\gcd(p,q) = 1$. Then $p^2 = 2q^2$, so $p$ is even; write $p = 2k$. Then $4k^2 = 2q^2$, i.e. $q^2 = 2k^2$, so $q$ is also even. This contradicts $\gcd(p,q)=1$. $\blacksquare$

So there is **no** $c \in [0,2] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ with $f(c) = 0$, although such a $c$ would be required by the IVT.

---

## A Sharper Illustration

The failure is even more striking with
$$g : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}, \qquad g(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } x^2 < 2, \\[2pt] +1 & \text{if } x^2 > 2. \end{cases}$$

- $g$ is **continuous on $\mathbb{Q}$**: for every rational $x_0$, we have $x_0^2 \neq 2$, so $g$ is locally constant near $x_0$.
- $g(0) = -1$ and $g(2) = +1$.
- $g$ never takes the value $0$, even though $-1 < 0 < 1$.

A continuous rational-valued function on $\mathbb{Q}$ can therefore *jump* over an entire range of values.

---

## Why This Happens

The IVT is logically equivalent (over the ordered field axioms) to the **completeness** of $\mathbb{R}$ — every nonempty subset bounded above has a least upper bound.

The set $\{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 2\}$ is bounded above in $\mathbb{Q}$ but has **no rational supremum**: the natural candidate $\sqrt{2}$ does not exist in $\mathbb{Q}$. The "hole" at $\sqrt{2}$ is precisely the gap through which $f(x)=x^2-2$ slips from negative to positive without ever vanishing.

$$\boxed{\text{IVT } \Longleftrightarrow \text{completeness of the underlying ordered field.}}$$

Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is not complete, the IVT cannot hold there.

data.title: Galois group governing variety cohomology theories

data.prompt: Can you lay the groundwork for understanding the problem of a motivic Galois theory?
data.response:
# The Setup for Motivic Galois Theory

The problem of motivic Galois theory is, at its heart, the dream of a **single Galois-theoretic structure** that governs the cohomology of algebraic varieties — generalizing classical Galois theory of number fields and unifying the disparate cohomology theories that arise in algebraic geometry. To appreciate the problem, we need to walk through several layers.

## 1. Classical Galois theory as a starting point

Recall that for a Galois extension $L/K$, the group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ encodes the symmetries among algebraic relations. Most importantly:

$$G_\mathbb{Q} := \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$$

is the absolute Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}$ — a profinite object whose representations are the central objects of modern number theory.

The first key idea is that **a group can be recovered from its category of representations**. This is Tannaka–Krein duality.

## 2. The Tannakian formalism

A *neutral Tannakian category* over a field $k$ is, roughly, a $k$-linear abelian tensor category $\mathcal{T}$ equipped with a fiber functor $\omega: \mathcal{T} \to \mathrm{Vec}_k$ that is exact and tensor-preserving. The fundamental theorem says:

$$\mathcal{T} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}_k(G), \qquad G = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega).$$

That is, $G$ — an affine group scheme over $k$ — is reconstructed as the automorphisms of the fiber functor.

This is powerful because **we may have a category with the right formal structure but no group in sight**; the formalism then *defines* the group for us.

## 3. Cohomology of algebraic varieties

For a smooth projective variety $X$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, several cohomology theories coexist:

- **Betti**: $H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Q})$ — singular cohomology of complex points.
- **Algebraic de Rham**: $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\mathbb{Q})$ — hypercohomology of $\Omega^\bullet_{X/\mathbb{Q}}$.
- **$\ell$-adic étale**: $H^*_\mathrm{\acute{e}t}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)$ — carries a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-action.

These are linked by **comparison isomorphisms**, e.g.

$$H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Q}) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C} \;\xrightarrow{\sim}\; H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C}.$$

Each theory looks "different" but produces the same Betti numbers, the same Hodge numbers (roughly), the same $L$-functions. Why?

## 4. Periods: where the action is

The Betti–de Rham comparison, written in $\mathbb{Q}$-rational bases on each side, yields a matrix of complex numbers: the **periods** of $X$.

Key examples:
- $X = \mathbb{G}_m$: the period $\int_{|z|=1} \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i$.
- $X$ an elliptic curve: the periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$ of an invariant differential.
- $X = \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0,1,\infty\}$: iterated integrals give $\zeta(n)$ and multiple zeta values.

These numbers occupy a fascinating middle ground between algebraic and transcendental, and one quickly suspects there is a *symmetry group* governing the relations among them.

## 5. Grothendieck's vision: motives

Grothendieck proposed there should be a **universal cohomology theory** through which all others factor. Concretely:

- A category $\mathcal{M}(k)$ of motives over $k$.
- A functor $h: \mathrm{Var}(k) \to \mathcal{M}(k)$.
- Each cohomology theory $H^*_?$ factors as a *realization functor* $\mathcal{M}(k) \to (\text{stuff})$.

For pure motives (smooth projective $X$), one builds objects out of pairs $(X, p)$ where $p$ is an idempotent algebraic correspondence, and morphisms are correspondences modulo a chosen equivalence (rational, homological, numerical). The choice matters: only with the **standard conjectures** does one obtain an abelian, semisimple, neutral Tannakian category.

For mixed motives (general $X$), one wants a much richer category — the existence of an abelian category $\mathrm{MM}(k)$ remains conjectural, though Voevodsky constructed a beautiful triangulated version $\mathrm{DM}(k)$.

## 6. The motivic Galois group

Suppose we have $\mathcal{M}(k)$ as a neutral Tannakian category, with the Betti realization $\omega_B$ as fiber functor. Then we obtain:

$$G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k) := \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega_B),$$

a pro-algebraic group over $\mathbb{Q}$ — the **motivic Galois group**.

Expected features:
- Each motive $M$ gives a representation $G_{\mathrm{mot}} \to \mathrm{GL}(\omega_B(M))$.
- The classical Galois group $G_\mathbb{Q}$ should appear (e.g., as $\pi_0$ of $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$, or related quotients).
- For the subcategory of mixed Tate motives over $\mathbb{Z}$, $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$ is fairly explicit and intimately tied to multiple zeta values (work of Deligne, Goncharov, Brown).

## 7. The problems, sharply stated

Now we can articulate what "the problem of motivic Galois theory" really is:

**(a) Constructing the category.** Build $\mathcal{M}(k)$ — pure or mixed — as an abelian, neutral Tannakian category. For pure motives, this requires the standard conjectures (Künneth, Hodge type, etc.). For mixed motives, even formulating the correct $t$-structure on $\mathrm{DM}(k)$ is a major open problem.

**(b) The period conjecture.** Grothendieck's conjecture asserts that for a motive $M$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, the transcendence degree of the field generated by its periods equals $\dim G_{\mathrm{mot}}(M)$. This is an *enormous* generalization of Lindemann–Weierstrass and remains wide open even in seemingly basic cases — e.g., the algebraic independence of $\pi$ and $\zeta(3)$.

**(c) Computing $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$.** Even granting the framework, identifying the motivic Galois group of specific motives or sub-Tannakian categories is a deep question. Successes (Tate motives, certain hypergeometric motives) have driven enormous activity at the interface of number theory, mathematical physics (Feynman integrals), and combinatorics (Hopf algebras of MZVs).

**(d) Galois action and arithmetic.** How does $G_\mathbb{Q}$ sit inside $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$? The Mumford–Tate conjecture, the Tate conjecture, and the Hodge conjecture are all shadows of how restrictive the motivic Galois group should be — predictions about which $\ell$-adic or Hodge-theoretic structures actually come from algebraic geometry.

---

The unifying picture: **classical Galois theory is the Galois theory of zero-dimensional varieties (number fields). Motivic Galois theory is what you get when you allow varieties of arbitrary dimension and try to understand the symmetries among all their cohomological invariants simultaneously.** The "problem" is that this beautiful picture is, even today, only partially constructed — and the parts that work shed light on some of the deepest questions in mathematics.

The construction requires solving several deep problems: building a proper category of mixed motives, establishing the standard conjectures for pure motives to form a Tannakian category, and proving the period conjecture that connects the motivic Galois group to transcendence properties of periods. For tractable subcategories like Tate motives, the motivic Galois group is well-defined and relates to multiple zeta values, but for all motives over Q it remains conjectural. I'm thinking about how to structure this exposition—starting from classical Galois theory and the Tannakian perspective, then moving through cohomology theories and periods, before building up to what motives should be and why the Galois group matters. - Betti cohomology gives topological information when the variety is defined over the complex numbers, de Rham uses algebraic differential forms, ℓ-adic étale cohomology works over any field, and crystalline cohomology handles positive characteristic. Each satisfies the standard axioms for a Weil cohomology theory.

These appear in concrete examples like the 2πi from the punctured line, the lattice generators of an elliptic curve, and special values of zeta functions and polylogarithms - all mysterious transcendental numbers with deep arithmetic meaning.

If the category of motives forms a Tannakian category, it yields a motivic Galois group whose representations recover all the standard cohomology theories, and the Galois group of the rationals should embed into it. The period conjecture would then bound the dimension of this group by the transcendence degree of the periods themselves.

The main obstacles are that constructing motives rigorously requires unproven standard conjectures, mixed motives only exist in triangulated form so far, and the period conjecture vastly generalizes classical transcendence results - with specific cases connecting to multiple zeta values and Feynman integrals in physics.

data.jsonPrompt:
{
    "model": "claude-opus-4-7",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Can you lay the groundwork for understanding the problem of a motivic Galois theory?"
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "# The Setup for Motivic Galois Theory

The problem of motivic Galois theory is, at its heart, the dream of a **single Galois-theoretic structure** that governs the cohomology of algebraic varieties — generalizing classical Galois theory of number fields and unifying the disparate cohomology theories that arise in algebraic geometry. To appreciate the problem, we need to walk through several layers.

## 1. Classical Galois theory as a starting point

Recall that for a Galois extension $L/K$, the group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ encodes the symmetries among algebraic relations. Most importantly:

$$G_\mathbb{Q} := \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$$

is the absolute Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}$ — a profinite object whose representations are the central objects of modern number theory.

The first key idea is that **a group can be recovered from its category of representations**. This is Tannaka–Krein duality.

## 2. The Tannakian formalism

A *neutral Tannakian category* over a field $k$ is, roughly, a $k$-linear abelian tensor category $\mathcal{T}$ equipped with a fiber functor $\omega: \mathcal{T} \to \mathrm{Vec}_k$ that is exact and tensor-preserving. The fundamental theorem says:

$$\mathcal{T} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}_k(G), \qquad G = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega).$$

That is, $G$ — an affine group scheme over $k$ — is reconstructed as the automorphisms of the fiber functor.

This is powerful because **we may have a category with the right formal structure but no group in sight**; the formalism then *defines* the group for us.

## 3. Cohomology of algebraic varieties

For a smooth projective variety $X$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, several cohomology theories coexist:

- **Betti**: $H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Q})$ — singular cohomology of complex points.
- **Algebraic de Rham**: $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\mathbb{Q})$ — hypercohomology of $\Omega^\bullet_{X/\mathbb{Q}}$.
- **$\ell$-adic étale**: $H^*_\mathrm{\acute{e}t}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)$ — carries a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-action.

These are linked by **comparison isomorphisms**, e.g.

$$H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C}), \mathbb{Q}) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C} \;\xrightarrow{\sim}\; H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{C}.$$

Each theory looks "different" but produces the same Betti numbers, the same Hodge numbers (roughly), the same $L$-functions. Why?

## 4. Periods: where the action is

The Betti–de Rham comparison, written in $\mathbb{Q}$-rational bases on each side, yields a matrix of complex numbers: the **periods** of $X$.

Key examples:
- $X = \mathbb{G}_m$: the period $\int_{|z|=1} \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i$.
- $X$ an elliptic curve: the periods $\omega_1, \omega_2$ of an invariant differential.
- $X = \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0,1,\infty\}$: iterated integrals give $\zeta(n)$ and multiple zeta values.

These numbers occupy a fascinating middle ground between algebraic and transcendental, and one quickly suspects there is a *symmetry group* governing the relations among them.

## 5. Grothendieck's vision: motives

Grothendieck proposed there should be a **universal cohomology theory** through which all others factor. Concretely:

- A category $\mathcal{M}(k)$ of motives over $k$.
- A functor $h: \mathrm{Var}(k) \to \mathcal{M}(k)$.
- Each cohomology theory $H^*_?$ factors as a *realization functor* $\mathcal{M}(k) \to (\text{stuff})$.

For pure motives (smooth projective $X$), one builds objects out of pairs $(X, p)$ where $p$ is an idempotent algebraic correspondence, and morphisms are correspondences modulo a chosen equivalence (rational, homological, numerical). The choice matters: only with the **standard conjectures** does one obtain an abelian, semisimple, neutral Tannakian category.

For mixed motives (general $X$), one wants a much richer category — the existence of an abelian category $\mathrm{MM}(k)$ remains conjectural, though Voevodsky constructed a beautiful triangulated version $\mathrm{DM}(k)$.

## 6. The motivic Galois group

Suppose we have $\mathcal{M}(k)$ as a neutral Tannakian category, with the Betti realization $\omega_B$ as fiber functor. Then we obtain:

$$G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k) := \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega_B),$$

a pro-algebraic group over $\mathbb{Q}$ — the **motivic Galois group**.

Expected features:
- Each motive $M$ gives a representation $G_{\mathrm{mot}} \to \mathrm{GL}(\omega_B(M))$.
- The classical Galois group $G_\mathbb{Q}$ should appear (e.g., as $\pi_0$ of $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$, or related quotients).
- For the subcategory of mixed Tate motives over $\mathbb{Z}$, $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$ is fairly explicit and intimately tied to multiple zeta values (work of Deligne, Goncharov, Brown).

## 7. The problems, sharply stated

Now we can articulate what "the problem of motivic Galois theory" really is:

**(a) Constructing the category.** Build $\mathcal{M}(k)$ — pure or mixed — as an abelian, neutral Tannakian category. For pure motives, this requires the standard conjectures (Künneth, Hodge type, etc.). For mixed motives, even formulating the correct $t$-structure on $\mathrm{DM}(k)$ is a major open problem.

**(b) The period conjecture.** Grothendieck's conjecture asserts that for a motive $M$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, the transcendence degree of the field generated by its periods equals $\dim G_{\mathrm{mot}}(M)$. This is an *enormous* generalization of Lindemann–Weierstrass and remains wide open even in seemingly basic cases — e.g., the algebraic independence of $\pi$ and $\zeta(3)$.

**(c) Computing $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$.** Even granting the framework, identifying the motivic Galois group of specific motives or sub-Tannakian categories is a deep question. Successes (Tate motives, certain hypergeometric motives) have driven enormous activity at the interface of number theory, mathematical physics (Feynman integrals), and combinatorics (Hopf algebras of MZVs).

**(d) Galois action and arithmetic.** How does $G_\mathbb{Q}$ sit inside $G_{\mathrm{mot}}$? The Mumford–Tate conjecture, the Tate conjecture, and the Hodge conjecture are all shadows of how restrictive the motivic Galois group should be — predictions about which $\ell$-adic or Hodge-theoretic structures actually come from algebraic geometry.

---

The unifying picture: **classical Galois theory is the Galois theory of zero-dimensional varieties (number fields). Motivic Galois theory is what you get when you allow varieties of arbitrary dimension and try to understand the symmetries among all their cohomological invariants simultaneously.** The "problem" is that this beautiful picture is, even today, only partially constructed — and the parts that work shed light on some of the deepest questions in mathematics."
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Produce a PDF file presenting the previous response in the form of an interim research working paper."
                }
            ]
        }

    "stream": true,

                "skill_id": "pdf",
                "version": "latest"
            }
        ]
    },
    "beta": [
        "files-api-2025-04-14",
        "code-execution-2025-08-25",
        "skills-2025-10-02"
    ]
}
